title: Sigala, alone
tomorrow: the Kalamas have heard too many teachers. how do they decide?

lines: EAST, SOUTH, WEST, NORTH, DOWN, UP.
cards: Early morning outside a city. A young man named Sigala, hair and clothes still wet, is bowing: east, south, west, north, down, up. The Buddha, walking in for alms, asks him why.
Sigala says his father told him to, as he was dying. He doesn't know what it's for. He just keeps the promise.

teach.h: THE BUDDHA FILLS THE DIRECTIONS IN.
teach.b: The Buddha doesn't tell him to stop. He fills the directions in. In paraphrase: east is your parents.
South, your teachers. West, your partner and children. North, your friends.
Below, the people whose work supports you. Above, those who teach the spiritual life. Then the surprise of DN 31: every direction runs both ways.
Children care for their parents; parents keep children from harm and teach them a skill.
Students show up for teachers; teachers train them well and introduce them to good friends.
Friends keep their word and stay in hard times; the people who work for you are treated fairly and given rest.

teach.h: A MAP OF WHO HOLDS UP YOUR LIFE.
teach.b: So a bow turns into a map of everyone holding up your life, and of what you owe each of them. Now look back at the week's road. She chose.
The direct path. Sixteen steps. A mind like the earth.
Six lines, and today, six directions to carry them in.

how: The Sigalovada Sutta is taught in Theravada communities as guidance for lay life, and its six directions are often used to talk about family, school, friendship and work.

o: a monk who taught the Buddha how to meditate
the young man whose six bows became a map of his people
a king who gave the Buddha a park to teach in

games.q: the six directions — tap the pairs.
p: the people whose work supports you

s: the Buddha told Sigala to stop his father's ritual
he kept the bow and filled the directions in with people.
in DN 31, each direction comes with duties both ways
children care for parents; parents protect and teach children, and so on.
DN 31 is mainly for monks and nuns
it's advice for a householder: family, teachers, friends and work.

games.q: your new job's manager asks you to cover a shift on your day off, again. what fits DN 31?
o: duties run both ways: do your part, and ask for the rest owed to you
workers owe everything; say yes every time
it's only a job, so owe it nothing and walk away
games.why: in DN 31 every direction runs both ways. those who work for others give their best; those they work for treat them fairly and give them rest.

practice: Pick one direction: a parent, a teacher, a friend, someone whose work supports yours. Bring one person from it to mind, and one small duty you owe them. Sit with that person in view, as if bowing toward them.

wordCard.voice: Sigala: the young man of DN 31, whose dawn bow to six directions the Buddha turned into a map of the people in his life.

orig.note: Pali: direction, quarter of the sky. Sigala bows to six of them.

carryVoice: Six directions to carry home, and each one bows back to you. Two weeks of reading, gathered.
